analysis.one_liner: Extends federal child labor protections to children working on farms.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2007 and referred to committee, where it sat without a vote until Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal child labor law has long had a loophole: children of any age can work unlimited hours on farms as long as it is outside school hours, and 12-year-olds can legally do hazardous work in commercial agriculture with a simple waiver. The CARE Act would have closed those loopholes, barring most farm work for children under 14 (outside of family farms), raising the minimum age for dangerous farm work like operating machinery or handling pesticides from 16 to 18, and sharply increasing fines for employers who violate child labor rules. It would also have required employers to report serious injuries, illnesses, and deaths of farmworkers under 18 to the Labor Department. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children employed in commercial agriculture, who are currently exposed to dangerous machinery, pesticides, and long hours at ages far younger than children in any other industry, and their families. The bill also would have produced the first systematic federal data on farm injuries to children, which benefits anyone trying to measure and fix the problem.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exemptions that allow children under 16 to work unlimited hours in agriculture, permitting it only on a farm owned or operated by the child's own parent or guardian and only outside school hours [S2] [S3].
Raises from 16 to 18 the minimum age for hazardous agricultural work, such as operating machinery, and eliminates the waiver that let 12-year-olds be certified for hand-harvesting crops [S2] [S3].
Raises civil penalties for child labor violations from a $10,000 cap to as much as $50,000, and up to $100,000 for repeat or willful violations causing serious injury or death [S3].
Creates criminal penalties of up to five years in prison for employers whose repeated or willful child labor violations kill or permanently disable a worker under 18 [S3].

Requires employers to report serious injuries, illnesses, and deaths of farmworkers under 18 within five days, and directs the Labor Department to analyze injury data and report to Congress annually [S2] [S3].
Incorporates EPA pesticide-safety standards into the child labor rules, so children would have legal protection against pesticide exposure [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial agricultural employers, who rely on young workers for hand-harvesting crops and would face higher penalties, mandatory injury reporting, and a smaller pool of legal child labor.

drawbacks.text: Family farms would feel the change most: the bill preserves the exemption only for children working on a farm owned or operated by their own parent or guardian, so teenagers working on relatives' farms or neighbors' farms outside school hours would lose those jobs [S3].

The reporting and penalty provisions add compliance paperwork and financial exposure for farm employers, and penalty maximums rising tenfold could hit small operations hard for paperwork lapses, not just safety failures.

Critics of raising the hazardous-work age note that many farm tasks have long been treated as a normal part of rural adolescence; the bill's own construction preserves parental-farm work but still narrows paid seasonal work for rural 14- and 15-year-olds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is children's safety against a cheap, flexible seasonal labor supply for agriculture. Child farmworkers face machinery, sharp tools, heat, and pesticides at ages when children in every other industry are legally barred from such work, and Agriculture Department data cited in public debate has repeatedly shown farm work is among the most dangerous jobs for teens. The bill keeps the family-farm exemption intact, so the cost falls mainly on commercial growers who hire very young workers. The design is targeted, but its effect on small rural economies and teenage seasonal earnings is real and worth acknowledging.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucille Roybal-Allard (D-CA) and five Democratic colleagues introduced the CARE Act of 2007 on June 12, 2007 [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S5].
On July 24, 2007 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
Twenty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but no Republicans did, and the committee never reported it to the floor [S4] [S5].
The bill would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, the same statute that sets federal child labor rules for nonfarm industries [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial agricultural employers came out ahead: by the bill's death, the exemptions allowing young children to work long hours harvesting crops and the low penalties for violations remained in force. Rural families whose teenagers work farm jobs also avoided new restrictions.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled House.

industries.industry: Commercial agriculture, especially fruit and vegetable growers relying on hand harvesting
industries.note: The bill removes a legal supply of very young, low-paid farm labor and raises penalties up to tenfold for child labor violations, plus new injury-reporting duties. The industry's interest in keeping the current rules runs against children's safety, since the loopholes the bill closes are what allow underage exposure to machinery and pesticides.

The parent-owned-or-operated exemption survives, so children working their own family's farm are unaffected, but teenagers working nearby farms for wages would lose those jobs. Small farms also bear new reporting and penalty exposure when they hire young workers.
